chapter: Don Albert, Detroit and the Army
title: Joining Don Albert, Indianapolis, and the Detroit sextet
summary: Reason wins the job with Don Albert on an arrangement, stays to 1939, then leads a band in Indianapolis, works in Grand Rapids, and writes arrangements for a Detroit six-piece before induction.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: And, uh, he couldn't get any of them to play. And those were some of his special tunes. He figured they couldn't play that. They couldn't play anything else he had. So, when I went there, uh, I was still half asleep. So, he said, uh, play this for me. And, uh, I said, which, I said, this is the arrangement? He said, yeah. I said, man, I'm ready to rehearse right now. Let's go. And I went on it. And Don jumped up and Don, he said, this is what I've been trying to get you fellas to do all day. And the band is going to race. And I went on with Don. And I stayed with Don until 1939. And in 1939, we were working, uh, in Detroit on location. Uh, um, with, uh, at the, uh, Club Plantation, 555 East Adams Street. And, uh, I didn't like the salary. We had played in, in, in Indianapolis, Indiana. And, uh, uh, Joe Mitchell, Italian fellow owned the club there. And he told me, he said, look, anytime you want to leave that band, see, write me a postcard or send me, or call me, do anything, you see. And I sent for you to come. And I left, um, Don Alva's band. I gave him a two weeks notice. And I quit and went to Indianapolis, Indiana. And I sent back to New Orleans. And I took part of Joe Robey, she was being in there. And I sent for Sam Dutre, but Sam didn't want to come. He had, he was tied up with, um, uh, money and the bus. He had some money, it was willed to him, from, uh, Nora Dutre, his trombone player, from Chicago. And it will sound a lot of money. And he loaned Joe Robey showed some money to buy a new bus. And he didn't want to leave his money behind. And, uh, so he sent Seaman Jefferson, clarinet player. Uh, Dennis Gishard, those two. And Gene Ware, our trumpet player. Those three came up to, um, I sent for them. And they came to Indianapolis, Indiana. We worked on that one job until the first of, uh, 42. And, um, a fella got killed from the place. And they closed the place down. They didn't, he didn't, didn't take us off Saturday, but it was no more business. And I, I went to work with a band out of Grand Rapids. And, uh, Grand Rapids, Michigan. And while working with this little band, uh, Freddie Coleman and Ruben Hughes and Saul Broad, a Jewish fella. They came, they called New Orleans looking for me. And, uh, they said, he's in, last time we heard about Lionel, he was in Indianapolis, Indiana. So they contacted Indianapolis, Indiana, Union. And, uh, this union referred them to the Grand Rapids Union. And they said, yes, he's waking out here at the Celebrity Club. And, uh, they didn't even call me. They came up, Freddie Coleman, uh, Saul Broad and Ruben Hughes. They said, man, we need you bad in Detroit. They said, we had a band over here, over there. And the local boys, the half or half of the band, and they're fixing to go on a regular location. They had all of the arrangements. So they quit after rehearsing. The Detroit boys quit. And they were gonna pick up three more boys. And they were going on the job. He said, now, if you can come with us. I said, well, how many pieces are you gonna use there? He said, uh, we're gonna use six pieces. I need a bass player. I need a tenor saxophone player. And bass player and a tenor saxophone player. And I need you. I said, well, I'll tell you, when you go to Indianapolis, Indiana, and you get, you ask for, uh, I think this boy's name was Joe Williams. And, uh, ask for Seaman Jefferson. He was my tenor sax. And, uh, I'll meet you tomorrow evening in Detroit. When they got to Detroit, I had written three arrangements. I was ready for rehearsal. I sat up that night, and I wrote enough arrangements for that six piece band to keep us rehearsing two weeks. And that saved the day for us there. I stayed there. Freddie Coleman came back to New Orleans. And I was, um, um, I went, I went to the Army. I was inducted into the Army from this same job in 1943. I went in, went, they sent me to, uh, Battle Creek, Michigan. I stayed in Battle Creek, Michigan. They kept me there about six weeks playing with the, um, the MP band. And, um, I left, they sent me down to Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland. And when I got down there, um, I stayed there from 43 until April the 12th, 1946. They sent me to school for the mechanic. And after three and a half weeks, they, um, changed that. My MOS and sent me to, um, another school for the clay typists. And after my four weeks was up, they sent me on the field for field training down in, um, just below Richmond, Virginia. And, um, when I came back, the, uh, first sergeant said, I was, uh, the reason, pack up your, um, fatigues, check it in, check out your, uh, khaki suit, check out and, and, uh, just, um, get another set of khakis and another set of ODs and go to detachment E. For the duration of the war and one year after. That's just about two city blocks from where I was trained at.
